newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan bank denies split in top ranks.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan bank denies split in top ranks.

text.p: The Kenya Commercial Bank Group (KCB) on Monday denied reports of a split in its top ranks as brokers at the Nairobi Stock Exchange reported cautious trading with investors waiting for events to unfold at the bank.

The KCB board of directors called a news conference to deny local media allegations that differences between chairman and chief executive Alexander Kaminchia and general manager Elijah arap Bii had split management and was undermining performance.

"At no time has there been any corporate war or any conflict within the bank's top management. Consequently, there are no groupings or split in the board or senior management," senior Treasury official Njeru Kirira told reporters.
On Friday, the independent The People weekly newspaper spoke of an unfolding corporate war between Kaminchia and Bii. It said the sharp rift had put the bank's future in jeopardy.
Kaminchia described the report, which suggested he feared losing his position to Bii, as "lies and nonsense".
Asked whether he planned to leave his job, Kaminchia said: "I am not about to retire. This is a presidential appointment and I will retire at the president's leisure."
Nairobi Stock Exchange brokers said investors were treading cautiously in the wake of the reports, waiting for events to unfold. KCB eased to 94 from 95 in Monday trading.
"There's bound to be a slight shock in the market mainly out of panic but not for the long term," a senior broker said.

"The problem, however, is small and solvable and can easily be sorted out by the government. If politics gets in the way of sound management, it can easily do away with one of them (bank executives)," another broker said.
Kaminchia made no specific reference to the KCB stock.
The government owns 60 percent of KCB while 40 percent belongs to the public through the Nairobi Stock Exchange.

Market analysts said a majority of foreign investor interest in KCB was unlikely to be discouraged as the main logic behind their investment was a belief the share was undervalued. On Monday, foreign investors bought 20,900 shares at 95 and 94.50.

Early this month, KCB announced a seven percent rise in pre-tax profits to 4.045 billion shillings ($73.67 million) in the trading year to 31 December 1996 compared with 3.784 billion shillings in the previous year.
